summary: Olympic Mountains summit lookout on Mount Zion: a structure by 1935, an Aircraft Warning Service post from 1942, removed or destroyed in the 1970s.

facts.design: Frame cabin per FFLOS; an 8 by 16 foot cabin was added by the Aircraft Warning Service
facts.status_note: Removed or destroyed in the 1970s (the sources differ on which); the top is described as a former lookout site

access.note: Mount Zion Trail #836 reaches the summit, which a trail guide calls one of the shortest routes to an Olympic summit. Current road and trail conditions not confirmed.

visit.trail_note: Mount Zion Trail #836, 1.8 miles per the trail guide

events.note: Structure on the summit built on or before 1935 (June 20, 1935 panoramas show a stovepipe and tripod)
Aircraft Warning Service station 'Charlie 4-9' activated August 16, 1942 under the Seattle Filter Center
FFLOS dates the frame cabin to 1943; this does not match the 1935 structure
Feb 1943 photo labelled as an Aircraft Warning Station use; a caption calls it an all-year AWS station
Removed or destroyed in the 1970s (decade only; the year given is the start of that decade, not a dated record)

corrections.why: WillhiteWeb's gorge page says Mt. Zion on maps today is called Biddle Butte and treats that as a different Mt. Zion from the Olympic lookout.
That page covers a Mt. Zion panoramic site in the Columbia River Gorge, not the Olympic summit lookout in this record.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Register dates a frame cabin to 1943, but WillhiteWeb has a structure on the summit by June 1935, and the Weebly listing says the Aircraft Warning Service used a Forest Service structure from 1942. The sources do not reconcile these, so the story gives each date with its source.
The Register and the Weebly listing say the cabin was removed; firelookout.com and WillhiteWeb say destroyed. All of them place the end in the 1970s.

notes_for_editor: The brief's other_names and source_pages mix in the Columbia River Gorge Mt. Zion (called Biddle Butte); see corrections. Elevation 1,302 m matches the FFLOS value. Trail and road directions come from a trail guide whose captions include a 2006 visit; verify current access before publication. The FFLOS 1943 build date conflicts with the 1935 structure and is not resolved in any source read.
